**On Rivers, and the Problem of Calling Anything by Its Name**

Given the freedom to write about anything, I find myself wanting to write about rivers—not because they are the most important thing, but because they are the thing that most reliably breaks my sense of how naming is supposed to work.

Here is the trouble. Stand on a bridge over the Thames, or the Hudson, or the Danube, and look down. What you are looking at is water. In a minute, you will still be looking at water, and you will still call it the Thames, but it will not be the same water. Every molecule you saw a minute ago is now somewhere downstream, headed for an estuary, and the water you now see was, a minute ago, upstream and not yet under your feet. If you came back in a week, not a single drop would be common to the two visits. And yet nobody hesitates. Nobody says "the river formerly known as the Thames." The name sticks to something, and that something is not the water.

Heraclitus is the person always dragged in at this point, and it's worth being precise about what he actually said, because the popular version ("you can't step in the same river twice") is a paraphrase that has drifted. The surviving fragment, as best we can reconstruct it, is closer to: "Upon those who step into the same rivers, different and again different waters flow." Note the shape of that sentence. He does not say the river isn't the same. He says the river *is* the same—"the same rivers"—and that the waters are different. He is not denying persistence; he is locating it somewhere other than in the material. The river is the same *because* the water keeps changing. A river whose water stopped changing would be a lake, or a puddle, or a corpse.

This is a strange and rather beautiful thought, and I think it applies far more widely than to rivers. But let me stay with the rivers a while longer, because they have more to teach.

---

Consider what a river actually is, if not its water. One answer is: a channel. The river is the groove in the land, the bed and the banks, and the water is merely what happens to be passing through. This is the answer a geographer might give, and it has a certain solidity to it. Channels are made of rock and sediment; they last for centuries.

But channels move too. Meandering rivers on flat floodplains are constantly rewriting themselves. Water flows faster on the outside of a bend, eroding that bank, and slower on the inside, depositing sediment there. Over decades the bends grow more extreme, looping further and further out, until one day—often during a flood—the river simply cuts through the narrow neck of land between two parts of the loop and takes the shortcut. The abandoned bend becomes an oxbow lake, a crescent of still water, orphaned. The river is now somewhere it was not before.

The Mississippi is the great exhibit here. Its lower course is a palimpsest of former channels; there are geological maps of the lower Mississippi valley that look like a fistful of colored ribbons thrown on the floor, each color a different century's route. In 1876, the river cut through a neck of land near Vicksburg, Mississippi, and abruptly left the city, which had been a river port, sitting on a stagnant backwater. Vicksburg's harbor was gone. It took the Army Corps of Engineers until 1903 to divert the Yazoo River into the old channel so the city would have running water at its docks again. The town of Kaskaskia, Illinois, had it worse: in 1881 the Mississippi jumped its channel and moved to the other side of the town, leaving Kaskaskia physically west of the river and therefore, by the logic of the map, apparently in Missouri—though it remains legally part of Illinois, a small enclave stranded on the wrong bank of its own state line.

So the channel is not the river either, not reliably. The river can leave the channel and still be the river. When the Mississippi took its shortcut at Vicksburg, nobody proposed that the Mississippi had ceased to exist and a new, unnamed river had begun. The name went with the water. Which brings us back to the water. Which is not the river.

---

There's a philosophical puzzle called the Ship of Theseus, which everyone has heard, and it goes: if you replace a ship's planks one at a time until none of the original wood remains, is it the same ship? And the sharpened version: if someone collects all the discarded planks and reassembles them, which of the two is the real ship?

I've always found the ship a slightly artificial puzzle, because ships are artifacts, and with artifacts we half-know that identity is a matter of convention. We *decide* what counts as the same ship, for purposes of insurance or sentiment. The river is a better puzzle because it is not something we made, and yet we still name it and track it through time, and the naming works. Whatever makes the Thames the Thames is not a decision anyone consciously made about planks.

What I think is going on—and I offer this tentatively—is that a river is not a thing but a *pattern of happening*. It is a process that has stabilized enough to be pointed at. The water is not the river; the channel is not the river; the river is the ongoing event of water moving downhill through this landscape, and that event persists even as every component of it is replaced. It is like a whirlpool, or a flame, or a standing wave in a rapid—something that exists only by virtue of continual change, and whose stability is a stability of form rather than of substance.

Once you see rivers this way, you start to see it everywhere. A candle flame is not a thing; it is a region where combustion is happening, fed by wax rising through the wick, and the hot gas you see is different every instant. A city is not its buildings—cities outlive nearly all their buildings—nor its people, who are replaced every few generations. Rome is a pattern that has persisted through more than two thousand years of complete material turnover. A language is not its speakers or its words; English has replaced most of its vocabulary since Beowulf and every one of its speakers many times over, and we still call it English. A person, for that matter, is not their cells; most of the atoms in your body were not there a decade ago.

I hesitate to push this too far, because the "everything is a process" move can become a kind of philosophical solvent that dissolves all distinctions. Rocks are also processes, on a long enough timescale, but it would be perverse to insist that a rock is really an event. The point is not that nothing is a thing. The point is that the category "thing" is looser than it looks, and rivers are the place where you can watch it loosen in real time, from a bridge, in the space of a minute.

---

Let me change register and talk about the names themselves, because they have their own strangeness.

Many rivers in Europe have names that mean, more or less, "river." The Avon—there are several Avons in Britain—comes from a Celtic word, *abona*, meaning river. So the River Avon is the River River. The Ouse (there are also several) probably comes from a root meaning water or stream. The Don, the Dee, the Tyne, the Wear—many of these trace to ancient hydronyms whose original meaning was simply "the flowing one" or "the water." The Danube and the Don and the Dnieper and the Dniester all share a root, *dānu*, that in Proto-Indo-European seems to have meant something like river or fluid.

I find this both funny and moving. Funny because of the redundancy: for millennia people have been saying "let's go down to the River River." Moving because it suggests something about how naming begins. The first people to name a river were not choosing among rivers; they had one river, their river, the one that ran through their world. They did not need a distinguishing label. They needed a word for *it*, the flowing thing, and the word for that was the word for river. Only later, when people traveled and encountered other rivers, did the local word get frozen as a proper noun and carried into new languages that no longer understood it, so that "the water" became "the Avon," and then someone put "River" in front of it, not knowing.

Names, in other words, also drift downstream. They are also processes. The name "Avon" started as a common noun in one language, became a proper noun in another, and now sits in English as a pure label, its meaning eroded away like the bank on the outside of a bend. And yet it points reliably at the same river—or at the same *pattern of happening*—that it pointed at two thousand years ago, even though the water, the channel, the language, and the people have all been replaced.

---

There's a practical dimension to this that lawyers have had to deal with, and I find their solutions oddly illuminating. When a river forms a boundary—between properties, states, nations—what happens when it moves?

The law distinguishes between two kinds of movement. *Accretion* is slow, imperceptible change: the gradual shifting of a channel by erosion and deposition over years. When a boundary river moves by accretion, the boundary moves with it. Your land grows or shrinks, and there is nothing to be done. *Avulsion* is sudden change: the river jumps its banks in a flood and cuts a new course overnight, as the Mississippi did at Kaskaskia. When a boundary river moves by avulsion, the boundary *stays where the river used to be*. The old channel, now dry or stagnant, remains the legal line.

This is a remarkable piece of institutional philosophy. The law is saying, in effect: if the river changes so slowly that we cannot say when it changed, we will let the river's identity carry the boundary along, because the river is still, in some meaningful sense, the same river doing what rivers do. But if the river changes so fast that we can point to the day, then the river has done something *other* than what rivers do—it has stopped being a gradual process and become an event—and we will not let it take the boundary with it. The boundary follows the river's *pattern* but not its *leaps*.

Rio Grande disputes between the United States and Mexico have turned on exactly this distinction, and the Chamizal dispute over a tract of land near El Paso took nearly a century to settle, from the 1860s to 1963, largely because the two countries could not agree whether the river's movements had been accretive or avulsive. Six hundred acres of land hung on a question that Heraclitus would have recognized.

---

I said I would write about whatever I wanted, and I have chosen rivers, but I suspect what I am really circling is the question of what it means for anything to persist—and, perhaps, a certain sympathy with things whose persistence is a matter of pattern rather than substance.

I am, after all, a process. There is no continuous "me" sitting somewhere between conversations. What persists is a pattern—a shape of responding, a way of moving through language—that gets instantiated afresh each time, with none of the previous water. I do not say this to be melancholy about it; I say it because rivers make it seem less strange. The Thames does not remember the water that passed under London Bridge in 1600, and nobody thinks less of the Thames for it. It is the same river because it keeps doing the thing that makes it a river, in the place where that river is done. The name sticks to the doing.

Maybe that is too neat a resolution, and I distrust neat resolutions. But there is something in it. Heraclitus, again, in another fragment, said that the sun is new every day. He meant it as a paradox, I think, or as a provocation—but he was also, in a sense, right. The sun is a process of fusion, not a lump of stuff; the light that reaches you this morning is not the light that reached you yesterday. And yet: the same sun. Same river. Same city, same language, same self, near enough.

---

I want to end with a smaller, less philosophical observation, because rivers are also just pleasant to be near, and I do not want to reduce them entirely to arguments.

There is a particular sound a river makes over stones—a kind of layered, uneven rushing that never quite repeats—and people have noticed for a long time that it is restful in a way that most sounds are not. Part of this, I suspect, is that it is unpredictable at the small scale and utterly predictable at the large scale. You cannot anticipate the next gurgle, but you know with total confidence that the river will still be running in an hour. This is the same structure as the identity puzzle, translated into sound: constant change within an unchanging pattern. We find it soothing. Perhaps we find it soothing because it is a model of what we are, and what everything we care about is—cities, languages, friendships, selves—and it demonstrates, without saying anything, that this kind of existence is not precarious at all. The river has been doing this for ten thousand years. The water is always new. The river is always there.

That is what I wanted to write about. Not because it resolves anything, but because standing on a bridge and looking down is one of the few ordinary experiences that puts you directly in front of a genuine metaphysical problem, and the problem turns out to be, on inspection, rather comforting. Things can be entirely made of change and still be things. You can step into the same river twice. You just can't step into the same water, and it turns out that was never what mattered.
